Frontier biotech
in first‑class mail

Semaglutide was tested in thousands of people before any pharmacy could sell it.98 A vial of copper peptide powder skips that step: it comes in the post for $54 to $74, labelled “research use only”.78 Both are peptides, short chains of amino acids, the kind of molecule the body uses to send messages: insulin is one, and so are glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and oxytocin.1 Each message works like a key. It fits a receptor on a cell, turns it on at nanomolar concentrations, then falls apart into plain amino acids. That last step is the catch. Native GLP-1 is half gone in about 1.5 minutes,95 and a bare chain is digested in the gut, so chemists hung a fatty tail on semaglutide to park it on albumin, the blood’s own carrier protein; 1.5 minutes became a week, bought with a threefold drop in how tightly the drug grips its receptor.18 Nobody ran trials like that on the vial in the post. So this page asks two questions of every peptide it follows: does it work in people, and how would you know?

A peptide fits a receptor the way the body’s own hormone does

Why a peptide at all? Most drugs are small molecules, built to sit in a pocket; many of the body’s most important switches have no pocket to sit in. GLP-1’s receptor holds its hormone along a groove that runs the length of the contact, resolved to 2.1 Å by cryo-electron microscopy,111 and other targets are flat, wide faces where one protein meets another. Peptides fit because they are the messages those switches evolved to hold1,19 and because they hold tight, semaglutide sitting on that receptor at 0.38 nM.18

Those messages have had a name since 1902, when Emil Fischer joined two glycines and called the product a peptide, after peptone, digested protein, from the Greek for "cooked" (standard history, not retrieved here). Read literally, the name is already a definition: a piece of protein the size digestion leaves behind.

Digestion cuts one kind of link, the one every peptide is built from. Join the acid end of one amino acid to the amine end of the next and a water molecule leaves; that link is the peptide bond. Each amino acid is now a residue, a bead on a string (bond and term: standard chemistry, not retrieved here). Chemists use peptide loosely for any short chain, while the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) draws its line at 40 residues: one more and the same kind of molecule is a biological product, under a different law.2 With twenty kinds of bead, a 15-bead chain like BPC-157 is one of 2015≈3.3×1019 possible messages.

Each peptide’s effect begins
at its own address in the cell

Each of those messages needs an address. Picture every cell as a house, every door an address with its own lock, and peptides as keys the body cuts itself. Some knock at the door, as GLP-1 does at its receptor. Instead of knocking, some hold the furniture still: thymosin β4 grips actin, the cell’s scaffolding,94 and elamipretide sticks to cardiolipin, a fat in the mitochondrial membrane. Some walk right in: MOTS-c, which the mitochondria write themselves, gets as far as the kitchen (the mitochondrion), then the office (the nucleus), and it needs four greasy residues to pass that second door, because swapping them for alanines leaves it stuck outside.36 And some catch a bus, the blood protein albumin, and stay in town for a week. However it gets in, every visit starts a mechanism of action: the chain from where a drug binds to the change a body shows. Semaglutide’s chain ends in a long programme of randomised trials, BPC-157’s runs mostly through rats, and MOTS-c’s rests on a single trial of a close copy, in 20 adults. Every one of them starts at an address on this cell.

GLP-1 drugs worked in people,
and the money followed

Start with semaglutide’s class, the one that worked. After a meal, your gut texts “enough”. That text is GLP-1, a hormone that slows the stomach and makes you feel full, and tells the pancreas to release insulin only when blood sugar is high.19 Then it self-deletes: an enzyme called dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) clips the chain two residues in, and half the hormone is gone in about 1.5 minutes.95 Chemists made two moves. They swapped the residue DPP-4 cuts beside for one the enzyme cannot read, and they hung the fatty tail from the opening on a lysine, so the chain rides albumin instead of clearing; 1.5 minutes became a week, and 46 hours of half-life in a mini-pig.18 First came a drug from a Gila-monster venom peptide (1992);25 semaglutide and tirzepatide followed, and in 2026 retatrutide took off 19.0 to 28.3% of body weight across its dose groups at 80 weeks, against 2.2% on placebo, in 2,339 people.24,28 Money came with them: in 2025 the class earned Novo 206 bn Danish kroner (DKK) and Lilly $36.5 bn.6,7 Researchers followed this chain all the way into people, and every chapter here is measured against that.

what if the next GLP-1 drug is not a peptide?

People on orforglipron lose less weight than on the injectables: 11.2% of body weight at the highest dose tested, against 2.1% on placebo.27 Potency per molecule and the albumin trick are the peptides’ moat; the pill’s moat is the bottle, which needs neither a needle nor a fridge. Both will share a market that Novo now guides down 5 to 13% on price.6

That measure is a ladder, and every rung can fail, which is why so few molecules reach the top. GLP-1 drugs climbed all of them, from cells through animals and small human studies to randomised trials and approval.

Mitochondria write a hormone, MOTS‑c; only a copy reached a human trial

Lower down the ladder, the biology gets stranger. Mitochondria, the cell’s power plants, keep a tiny notebook of their own DNA, and in 2015 researchers reading a page everyone had taken for scaffolding, the 12S rRNA gene, found a message hidden inside it, sixteen beads long, since named MOTS-c.34 Exercise prints it. One bout of cycling raised it about 12-fold in the muscle of ten sedentary young men, and it was still raised four hours later.37,38 In the cell’s fluid it brakes the folate cycle, which switches on AMPK, the cell’s fuel gauge, so muscle burns fuel;34,35 when glucose runs short it walks to the office, the nucleus, and helps switch on antioxidant genes.36 In mice it falls with age, and treated mice handle insulin better.34,37

Old mice give the clearest result: at 22 months, treated ones ran 2.16 times as far on a treadmill as untreated, 19 animals against 18.37,38 People have had one trial, and of a close copy rather than the peptide itself: CB4211. Four weeks in 20 adults with obesity and fatty liver cut alanine aminotransferase (ALT), the enzyme a damaged liver leaks, by 21%, which is 25 points better than placebo, on 11 treated against 9 on placebo; weight only trended down.40 Twenty people is a hint at a direction, not a result.

Even so, MOTS-c matters. It is the clearest case of mitochondria talking back to the nucleus with peptides, the one shown to enter it,52,53 and it turns exercise into a drug target with a messenger the body already makes. For now that’s a research programme, not yet a product.

BPC-157 is a stomach-protein fragment tested almost only in rats

Already a product, BPC-157 is the chain turning at the top of this page: a 15-bead message cut from a stomach protein. It appears to work from outside cells. On blood-vessel cells it raises VEGFR2, the receptor for a growth signal, and blood came back faster in ischaemic rat legs, through more vessels than the untreated legs grew;29 on rat tendon cells it raises the growth-hormone receptor and primes JAK2, the kinase that receptor signals through.31,30 Nearly every paper on it since 1992 came from one lab, in Zagreb,17 while sellers pitch it for tendons, gut and joints. Its rodent record is large and consistent, and rats and dogs clear it in under half an hour, so whatever it does it does in a pulse.32 In people, the one fair test heard nothing above the noise: 53 patients over 14 days, a disease-activity index down 3.2 points on the drug against 1.6 on placebo, and a difference whose 95% confidence interval ran from −4.84 to 1.62, which includes no effect at all.13

In numbers, the human record is thin. PubMed holds about 200 BPC-157 studies,17 of which the FDA found five done in people, the only randomised one null and published only as an abstract.13 One tolerability study against placebo, 24 healthy subjects. Three clinic reports, 2 to 17 people each, no control group.17 Three adverse-event reports had reached the FDA’s database by December 2025. Reviewers found no cancer study at all, and the repeat-dose and DNA-damage studies they did find were run in animals, none of them covering the compounded product as it would be sold.13 So what can rats tell you? That the mechanism is worth a trial. Not that a tendon heals.

who says BPC-157 works, and who gains if it does?

With no positive trial on file, FDA scientists found the legal criteria "weigh against" adding BPC-157 to the compounding list: no evidence it works in ulcerative colitis, too little human safety data to characterise the risk, a risk of immune reactions to impurities and clumps in the powder (certificates at 97.8% and 98.3% purity, no endotoxin test), and animal toxicology that does not cover the product as it would be sold.13 Its advisory committee voted the other way on 23 July 2026,16 and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put BPC-157 on its enforcement-discretion list for injection under the skin or into muscle, by mouth and on the skin.14 From the clinic, a 2025 review of muscle and joint use reached the same place: promising animal data, no controlled human trial.33

Who would gain from a good trial? In February 2026 Undark and STAT reported that Sikirić has been named on BPC-157 patent applications since 1989. He is listed as an owner of PharmaCotherapia, which sponsored a 2015 trial whose data were submitted and then withdrawn from the registry, and as CEO of Diagen, which says it owns a patent on a stable form that is "currently for sale". None of this appeared on the papers they reviewed.17 Conflicts don’t make the biology wrong. They make a second lab worth wanting, and there is one, small, in Taiwan.

Beyond any lab, sport has ruled too: the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) named BPC-157 as an example under S0, non-approved substances, from 1 January 2022.10

On the skin or up the nose,
a peptide is read only where it lands

Tendon or gut, a needle is the usual price of a peptide. Semax skips it up the nose, Matrixyl and copper peptide on the skin; they barely reach the blood and need not: each is read where it lands. Semax is a fragment of the stress hormone ACTH, and in rat hippocampus it raises the brain-growth factor BDNF about 1.4-fold;57 its one human study retrieved here measured brain connectivity in 52 healthy adults against placebo, which is a long way from a stroke trial.102 Matrixyl and copper peptide work on the fibroblasts that make collagen.

Semax, evidence 2/5
Russian clinical use, and one resting-state fMRI study in 52 healthy adults.102 A blinded stroke or cognition trial outside Russia would move it; none was retrieved, and no study links Semax to ketamine tolerance.
Matrixyl, evidence 2/5
Small cosmetic trials on wrinkle depth. A drug-grade randomised trial would move it; none was retrieved.

Copper peptide, the powder in that first envelope, is GHK, glycine-histidine-lysine. Your blood already carries it, about 200 ng per mL at age 20 and, by an often-repeated figure, 80 by 60.51 It was found in human serum in 1973, keeping liver cells alive in a dish.49 GHK grips one copper ion, and the pair, GHK-Cu, is the copper tripeptide-1copper tripeptide-1, the ingredient-list name for GHK-Cu; as a drug, prezatide copper. C₁₄H₂₃CuN₆O₄⁺, 402.92 g/mol.72 on ingredient lists. Brands also sell GHK with a palmitoyl tail, a 16-carbon fatty acid that helps it into skin, as Pal-GHK (Figure 28).73

Copper peptide raises collagen output in cells;
intact skin barely lets it in

In cells, GHK raises output of collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycans and supports the fibroblasts that build skin.51 On cell studies alone, a 2025 review calls it “undoubtedly” an anti-wrinkle ingredient;73 in people, the same review finds “a surprising absence of clinical studies” of GHK-Cu or Pal-GHK.73 Skin is the bottleneck: water-loving GHK-Cu barely gets in, and intact human skin let almost none through in 9 hours.74

So how a serum is made probably matters more than the number on its label. Both labs tested GHK-Cu on excised human skin; Hostynek’s used a flow-through diffusion cell, a chamber that holds skin over a fluid and measures what gets through.

That lab, the one that saw copper cross, applied 0.68%, close to The Ordinary’s 1% and 1,360 times Good Molecules’ 5 ppm.80 A review adds that a bound metal or a fatty tail helps more get in, and that a peptide this water-loving and unstable is hard to formulate.73 No trial has pitted two formulas against each other on people, so a buyer has one number: the percentage on the label. And a percentage is not a trial.

The same tripeptide sells for $0.11 to $80 a milligram

Labels matter to the law too: the FDA sorts a cosmetic from a drug by what the seller says it does.75 So the same molecule sells legally as a face serum and, as a dry powder labelled “research use only”, on the grey market.

Thymosin β4 / TB-500

Binds actin monomers one for one and holds them, so actin cannot grow into a fibre.94 "TB-500" vials are commonly described as the 17–23 fragment Ac-LKKTETQ (secondary sources).

Human: RGN-259 eye drops: one phase 2 dry-eye randomised controlled trial (RCT), nine patients47; neurotrophic keratopathy SEER-1, n = 18, 6/10 vs 1/8 healed at 4 wk (p = 0.066).48 Not approved.

GHK-Cu

Gly-His-Lys, found in human serum in 1973, binds copper and drives wound and skin gene programmes in culture.49,50,51 The widely repeated "200 → 80 ng/mL from age 20 to 60" has no primary measurement study behind it that this review could find.

Human: cosmetic and wound studies, none retrieved here. Injectable nomination withdrawn.

CJC-1295

Growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) analogue whose maleimide tail bonds to the one free thiol on albumin, Cys34cysteine, residue 34.99 Half-life 5.8–8.1 days; GH 2–10× for six days or more and IGF-1 1.5–3× for nine to eleven days, with IGF-1 still above baseline at 28 days, in healthy adults.41

Human: two randomised dose-escalation trials, 2006. Nomination withdrawn; not listed by HHS.

Ipamorelin

Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH₂; the first GHRP-receptor agonist as selective for GH as GHRH itself, leaving ACTH and cortisol unmoved, in pigs and rats.42

Human: no efficacy trial retrieved. Ipamorelin acetate remains in FDA Category 2 for 503B outsourcing facilities.11

Tesamorelin

Unlike CJC-1295, this GHRH analogue was approved: Egrifta, 10 November 2010, to reduce visceral fat in HIV lipodystrophy, on two phase 3 trials.43 Proof that the GH-axis peptides can clear the bar when someone runs the trials.

Elamipretide (SS-31)

D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH₂ concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane and binds cardiolipin, re-energising ischaemic mitochondria in rats.44,45

Human: accelerated approval 19 September 2025 (Forzinity) for Barth syndrome on knee-extensor strength gained in TAZPOWER’s open-label part; continued approval may hang on a confirmatory trial. Potentially a first-in-class drug, aimed at the inner mitochondrial membrane.46

Humanin and the SHLPs

MOTS-c's older sibling: a 24-residue peptide from the 16S rRNA gene, found in 2001 as a factor that rescued neurons from Alzheimer's-gene toxicity;52 six small humanin-like peptides (20–38 aa) followed.53

Human: none retrieved. Not on FDA’s category 2 or withdrawn-nomination lists.

Bremelanotide (PT-141)

Melanocortin agonist approved 21 June 2019 (Vyleesi) for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women; effect modest versus placebo in two 24-week trials, 1,247 women.54

Epitalon

Tetrapeptide from the Khavinson school. In 2025, telomerase activity rose 4× in IBR.3 fibroblasts and 26× in HMEC cells, with longer telomeres, in culture.55,56

Human: none retrieved. HHS draft lists it for intermittent SC/IM courses (insomnia was the PCAC indication).

Semax (and Selank)

Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro raises BDNF and TrkB in rat hippocampus;57 Selank, its stablemate from the same school, was read beside it in the one human study this page retrieved.102 That study, and the clinical use behind both, are Russian.

Human: one resting-state fMRI study, 52 healthy adults, measuring brain connectivity against placebo.102 HHS draft lists Semax intranasal.

KPV

Lys-Pro-Val: the last three beads of α-MSH, whose chain ends SYSMEHFRWG‑KPV.100 Oral KPV reduced DSS and TNBS colitis in mice through the PepT1 di/tripeptide transporter.58

Human: FDA found no human exposure data.11 HHS draft: topical and oral.

AOD-9604

Residues 177 to 191 from the tail of human growth hormone, plus one tyrosine, reported to copy the hormone’s fat burning without its effect on blood sugar.101 Its 2007 phase 2b obesity trial missed its endpoint and development ended, a result known mainly through company disclosures (secondary sources). Nomination withdrawn.

Thymosin α1

Thymalfasin, Zadaxin: in trials for hepatitis B and C with mixed results, and not approved by the FDA.59 Nomination withdrawn.

The best-proven peptides all had
an owner who paid for trials

Sorted by proof in people instead of price, the table runs from dark to pale. At the pale end sits the new list from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). None of its peptides scores above 3; its 3s were earned by a close copy, CB4211, and by eye drops of the parent protein, RGN-259, whose best randomised result healed 6/10 eyes against 1/8 on placebo in 18 patients, at p = 0.066.48 Neither is the vial on sale.

Half-life ranks these peptides a second way: not by how much proof there is, but by how cheaply the next piece could be bought. Nine of them have a published figure, eight measured in people and BPC-157’s in rats and dogs,32 and every figure longer than a day belongs to an engineered molecule — a fatty-acid chain or an albumin linker bought those days. Of the ten without one, two are this page’s own gap: elamipretide and thymosin β4 have both been measured in people and the numbers are simply not here. Elamipretide’s label is the stranger of the two, reporting how fast the drug is absorbed, where it spreads and how it leaves, and never how long it lasts.137 The other eight are the record’s gap rather than ours: no human half-life has ever been published for them. MOTS-c is the sharpest case, nominated for compounding as an injection while nobody has given the native peptide to a person at all, and epitalon and KPV sit on the same list. Both mitochondrial peptides here, MOTS-c and humanin, have been measured in people only at rest, as the trace the body keeps of its own: nobody has injected a dose and watched it clear. That is the cheapest experiment in the table — a dozen volunteers, one injection, a morning of blood draws, no efficacy endpoint to argue over — and it is the one nobody has run. The figures added here are the VYLEESI135 and EGRIFTA SV136 labels, retatrutide’s phase 1b,138 a 1999 infusion study in healthy men for ipamorelin139 and, for thymosin α1, the monograph its row already cited;59 thymosin β4’s own volunteer studies report no figure at all.140

Made in days, a peptide chain leaves the factory
in different envelopes

Vials sold online typically start life as a necklace. Chemists thread amino acids one at a time onto a plastic bead in a tank, then cut the chain loose, wash it and freeze-dry it;107,108 a 15-bead peptide is fifteen turns of the loop. Biology has a second way, the one used for human insulin: hand the gene to a living cell and let it brew.107 A pharmacy pen is usually brewed, then finished by chemistry. Either way the chain is done in days (typical times, marked as estimates in Figure 15). What differs is the envelope: the same kind of molecule can leave the factory as a branded pen, a pharmacist’s vial or a website’s “research only” vial. Which envelope is the vial in the post?

Money follows every envelope, factories first. Novo Holdings paid $16.5 bn for Catalent in December 2024;61 Pfizer paid about $10 bn for Metsera's obesity pipeline in November 2025.62 Meanwhile, CordenPharma committed about €900 M over three years to peptide capacity, on GLP-1 contracts it puts at €3 bn.106,63 Analysts put the 2025 peptide-drug market anywhere from $50 to 101 bn.65,66 At the other end, crypto payments to grey-market vendors went from $12 M to $32 M in one quarter, a 159% jump and a pace above $100 M a year.60,105

what to do before you buy
  1. Divide before you buy. Compare price per milligram of copper peptide, as Figure 14 does, not price per bottle.
  2. Read the label’s number. “10%” on a Matrixyl bottle is the share of a supplier’s solution.
  3. Check the legal door first. For injectables, a draft from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) lets 503A503A the section of US drug law for pharmacies that compound a medicine for one named patient, on a prescription pharmacies compound six peptides, which stay unapproved drugs; comments closed 13 November 2026, docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496.14
  4. Treat a seller’s certificate as the seller grading itself. Finnrick publishes outside tests; Penguin’s record there is 6/10, on two GLP-1 peptides rather than the skin peptides.84
  5. Watch for a GLP-1 under a code name, sold with mixing water. FDA warned a seller about one in March 2026.85
  6. California reaches further than federal law. On a plain reading, its 2026 synthetic-cannabinoid definition covers ART27.13, one of Everychem’s compounds, though the same section lets the substances be obtained for bona fide research.87
  7. Ask for the trial. Cells say yes and faces have not been asked. Hostynek’s skin test above came from the University of California, San Francisco, across town from the shop that sells Good Molecules.80,82

Most claims here hold
in a rat, in one lab, for a molecule, not a vial

So how would you know? Ask any peptide claim three things: which species, how many labs, and what else is in the vial.

Ask the species. Most peptide claims are true — in a rat. Human trials have to meet a standard: for ulcerative colitis the FDA’s is a modified Mayo score over at least a year.13 BPC-157’s ran two weeks and reported a composite index its abstract did not define.

Then count the labs. One group’s result is a hypothesis with good press. BPC-157’s second group is small, and in Taiwan, the source of the tendon papers above;17,31 even MOTS-c’s human exercise data come from the discovering lab’s own collaboration.37

Last, separate the molecule from the vial. What worries the FDA is the roughly 2% of a compounded powder that isn’t the sequence: chains cut short, beads flipped to their mirror image, clumps and bacterial endotoxin.13 Certificates showing 98% purity say nothing about the other 2%. Neither does “research use only”: printing it takes no test at all. No label can tell you what is in any one vial, and this page cannot either. Nothing can, short of opening it and testing.

Testing need not cost the wonder. MOTS-c, a 16-bead hormone written inside a ribosome gene and read by the nucleus under stress, is a new kind of biology, found only in 2015.34,36 As a class, peptides deserve the excitement; each molecule has to earn it.

Which of the six peptides on the HHS interim access list14 will get its trial first, and who will pay for it?

Until someone pays for that trial, the vial in the post holds the same kind of molecule as the drugs that worked, and almost none of the proof behind them. Chemists can make the molecule in days; the proof is a chain of evidence, from cell to rat, rat to person, one lab to a second, and for most of these peptides nobody has finished it.

Read the species, count the labs, test the vial.

what this page does not claim, and why

Appendix

Everything this page set aside sits below: figures and tables the story can do without, each with its caption and sources.

the words this page uses

Definitions are settled chemistry and pharmacology; an entry with a marker carries a retrieved source.

peptide
A short chain of amino acids. ≤ 40: a drug. > 40: a protein.2
peptide bond
The amide C(=O)–NH between residues; the link proteases cut.
residue
One amino acid inside a chain; its side chain R sets its chemistry.
half-life, t½
Time for the blood level to halve. Native GLP-1: 1.5 minutes.95 Semaglutide, with its fatty tail: about a week.18
agonist
A molecule that fits a receptor and switches it on.
oral bioavailability
The share of a swallowed dose that reaches blood. Peptides: very low without an absorption enhancer.23,67
immunogenicity
The chance antibodies form against the drug or its impurities.
503A
US rule letting a pharmacy compound a prescription from a listed bulk substance; six peptides are allowed meanwhile under interim enforcement discretion.14
GPCR
G-protein-coupled receptor: the class of switch GLP-1’s receptor belongs to.
cAMP
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate: the second messenger such a receptor raises inside the cell.
DPP-4
Dipeptidyl peptidase 4: the enzyme that cuts GLP-1 two residues in.95
mtDNA
Mitochondrial DNA: the small genome inside the mitochondrion, where MOTS-c is written.34
RCT
Randomised controlled trial: people put by chance into the drug group or the control group.
SC, IM
Subcutaneous and intramuscular: under the skin, into muscle. The routes in the tables above.
aa
Amino acids: how many beads are in the chain.
API
Active pharmaceutical ingredient: the drug itself, before it is put into a pen or a vial.
GMP
Good manufacturing practice: the quality system a medicine’s batch has to be made under.
CDMO
Contract development and manufacturing organisation: the company that makes a drug for whoever owns it.
RUO
"Research use only": a label on a vial, not a test anyone ran.
what a peptide’s length and its lipid tail buy, and cost
pill, peptide, antibody: the same questions asked of each

Think of a pill as a key: small, cheap, swallowable, fits one lock, sometimes the wrong one. Antibodies are hands: big, precise, grab anything on the outside, must be infused, cost a fortune. Peptides are notes: nature's own words, cheap to print, read only by the right cell, but they dissolve in minutes unless you laminate them.95,107

why does a peptide make a good drug?
1 the body already wrote the message
Insulin, GLP-1, oxytocin, GHRH, α-MSH are peptides.1,99,100,107 Copy the hormone, edit two residues, and you start from nanomolar potency and decades of physiology.
why potency comes cheap
2 sequence is code, SPPS is the compiler
Swap a residue (Aibα-Aminoisobutyric acid: alanine with a second methyl on the α-carbon. Knudsen and Lau call it the one substitution that both resisted DPP-4 and kept receptor affinity. It is the dashed bead in the sequence strings on this page.), add a fatty tail (semaglutide's is C18)107, close a ring, use a D-amino acid: standard modules, same reactor. Retatrutide hits three receptors from one chain.28
why iteration is fast
3 clean exit
A peptide is metabolised to amino acids: no reactive metabolites, little liver-enzyme interaction, low off-target toxicity compared with a new small molecule.
general pharmacology, not retrieved
4 the business case
Cents to make, patentable as an edited sequence, approved through the drug (NDA) path at ≤ 40 residues2, and priced like a biologic.
Figure 23
5 new biology keeps arriving
Mitochondrial DNA hides short reading frames (MOTS-c, humanin); the nuclear genome holds further unannotated short ORFs. Each is a candidate message.
Lee 201534, Hashimoto 200152
6 the catch
Delivery and half-life. The hot peptides are the ones where those were solved (GLP-1); the grey ones are the ones where they were not.

what this page does not claim, and why

GHK's "200 → 80 ng/mL" plasma decline: repeated in reviews, no primary measurement found. BPC-157 "stable in gastric juice": asserted, not measured in a retrieved study. Oral semaglutide "~1% bioavailability": commonly quoted, not confirmed in the retrieved paper. Tirzepatide's residue letters and the Selank sequence: from memory, so omitted. MOTS-c's WADA status: secondary sources only. Reference 10's WADA PDF is a national agency's hosted copy of the WADA list. Market-size figures are analyst estimates, shown as a range. Secondary reports are the only source for the 2024-12 warning-letter date and the "19 peptides" count of September 2023; FDA's own page confirms the 29 Sep 2023 date for several of them.

Peptide Atlas, one self-contained HTML file, inline SVG, structures drawn with RDKit 2025.09 from the sequences (scripts/structures.py). Educational review; not medical advice. Written 5 November 2026; checked for citations, legibility at 1280 and 400 px in light and dark, and the design budget.
